pros: Extremely simple and fast to compute (O(1) per pair)
Captures fundamental 'rich get richer' network dynamics
No parameters to tune or optimize
Works well for growing networks where popularity drives connections
Explains emergence of scale-free degree distributions
Computationally trivial compared to neighbor-set methods
Naturally handles directed graphs with in/out-degree variants
Provides theoretical foundation for network growth models
Scores are straightforward to interpret and rank
Useful baseline for comparing more complex prediction algorithms
Robust to missing data (only needs degree, not full neighborhood)
cons: Ignores shared context and common neighbors entirely
Zero score for degree-zero nodes (cold start problem)
Cannot capture triadic closure or community structure
Performs poorly in networks where homophily dominates
Assumes linear relationship (may not hold in practice)
Does not distinguish between different types of connections
Cannot identify unusual or unexpected connections
Biased toward existing high-degree nodes, reducing diversity
Less effective in static or slowly-evolving networks
